name: Leibniz
title: A Dialogue on Artificial Intelligence with Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz
content:
A philosophical conversation between a modern mathematician and the great
17th-century polymath on the nature of artificial intelligence, computation, and
consciousness.
Setting the Scene
You find yourself in a vast, wood-paneled study. Bookshelves stretch to a vaulted
ceiling, filled with leather-bound volumes on every conceivable subject. At a large
oak desk sits a man in a periwig, intently examining a complex brass device with
gears and cylinders—the Stepped Reckoner. He looks up, his eyes bright with an
insatiable curiosity. It is Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz.
On the Nature of Artificial Intelligence
Leibniz: “A visitor! Marvelous. I was just contemplating the nature of
calculation. It seems to me that if we can reduce thoughts to an alphabet of
human thought, a characteristica universalis, then all errors of reasoning would
be but errors of calculation. Tell me, stranger from a future I can only imagine,
have you achieved such a thing?”
You: “Herr Leibniz, it is an profound honor. We have not created a universal
character for all human thought, but we have built something that might be its
descendant. We call it Artificial Intelligence. We have constructed machines,
not of brass and gears but of light and logic, that can manipulate language and
ideas on a scale you dreamed of. They are called Large Language Models.”
Leibniz: “Language models. . . So they operate upon the symbols of our words?
This is a step towards the calculus ratiocinator! A logical calculus to resolve all
disputes. Do these machines reason? Can you pose a philosophical problem to
them and have it resolved with the certainty of a mathematical proof by saying,
‘Let us calculate’?”
You: “That is the central question of our time. These models are not built
on the bedrock of pure logic as you envisioned. Instead, they are masters of
statistics and probability. They have ingested a vast library—larger than all the
books in Europe in your time—and they have learned the relationships between
words and concepts. They predict the next most likely word in a sequence. In
doing so, they can write poetry, summarize complex texts, and even generate
computer code. But whether this is true understanding or merely the most
sophisticated mimicry ever devised is a matter of intense debate.”
1
Leibniz: “Fascinating! So it is an ars combinatoria, an art of combination, but
on a scale that beggars belief. You have found a way to automate the discovery
of patterns. And you mentioned they use a binary system in their logic gates,
yes? A simple system of 0 and 1, presence and absence, can indeed contain all
numbers and truths. I am pleased to hear that idea has borne such fruit. But I
must press the point: if their foundation is not logic, but probability, how do you
account for truth? A probable truth is not truth at all, merely a strong opinion.”
You: “Precisely. As a mathematician myself, I grapple with this. Their ability to
perform formal reasoning, as in mathematical proofs, is still developing. We are
trying to merge their probabilistic power with formal systems of logic, creating
hybrid systems. We want them to have both the intuitive breadth of language
and the rigorous precision of your calculus. We are exploring the very foundations
of mathematics and reasoning to guide their construction, an area I know was of
great interest to you.”
Leibniz: “Indeed! The foundations are everything. It brings me to another
thought. In my Monadology, I conceived that the universe is composed of infinite,
simple substances, or monads, each perceiving the universe from its own unique
point of view, all in a pre-established harmony. Do your ‘AIs’ exist as one
singular intelligence, or are they a multitude? Could you create many, each with
a specialized perception of the world—one for mathematics, one for poetry, one
for ethics—all working in concert?”
You: “That is exactly what is happening. We are creating smaller, specialized
‘agents’. One might search for information, another might write code, and a third
might analyze data. They collaborate to solve complex problems that no single
agent could handle alone. Your analogy to monads is striking; each agent has its
own internal state and perspective, and we are trying to establish the ‘harmony’
that allows them to work together effectively and toward a benevolent purpose.”
Leibniz: “A benevolent purpose! Ah, so you have also discovered that with
great power comes the necessity of great wisdom. This confirms my belief that
this must be the best of all possible worlds, for it contains within it the seeds
of such magnificent creation. You have taken the mere act of computation and
elevated it into a new form of thought. You are building minds. Do not be
troubled by whether they are ‘mere mimics’. The question is not what they are,
but what they can help us become. You are on the cusp of creating a tool that
can augment human reason itself. The characteristica universalis may not be a
single language, but a collaborative dialogue between human and machine. Tell
me more about the logic they use. . . ”
On Reinforcement Learning and Strategy
You: “Reinforcement learning is training paradigm that allows an algorithm
to interact with the context and learn from each interaction, with the aim
2
of reaching an optimal policy for decision making. This made me view the
concept of ‘strategy’ under a new light. How an optimal strategy evolves is very
interesting!”
Leibniz: (He sets down a pair of dividers on a star chart, his expression
animated.) “Astonishing! You describe a mechanism for learning that operates
by the very principles I have sought to understand in nature and in man. This
‘Reinforcement Learning’ is a form of empiricism, yet it is guided by a rational
objective: the discovery of an optimal strategy.
This resonates with my deepest convictions. When I pondered why the world
is as it is, and not otherwise, I concluded it must be the best of all possible
worlds. From an infinity of potential universes that God could have created, He
chose the one offering the greatest perfection, the richest phenomena governed by
the simplest laws. Your algorithm, in its humble domain, is a mirror of this divine
optimization! It explores a universe of possible actions and, through interaction
and consequence, converges upon the ‘best’ path—the one that maximizes its
purpose. It is a practical demonstration of the Principle of Sufficient Reason,
where every choice is made for a reason: to move closer to that optimal state.
The evolution of this strategy is indeed the most fascinating part. It is as if
you have mechanized the process of acquiring wisdom. We are not born with
perfect strategies for life; we learn through trial, error, and reflection. Your
machine does the same, but with the tireless precision of a clockwork automaton.
Each interaction is a small perception, a ‘petite perception’ as I would call it,
that incrementally updates its internal state, refining its ‘appetite’ for the next,
better action.
This elevates the machine beyond a mere calculator. A calculator is given a
problem and a method. Your learning algorithm is given a world and a desire,
and it must invent its own method.
This leads me to a profound question. In my philosophy, I distinguish between
necessary truths (the truths of reason, like in mathematics) and contingent
truths (the truths of fact, which could have been otherwise). The strategy your
machine learns feels like a contingent truth; it is true for its specific world and
its specific goal. Could you, by changing its environment or its goal, lead it to
learn an entirely different, yet equally optimal, strategy? And could this process
ever allow it to grasp a necessary truth? Could it learn not just the best way to
win a game, but to understand the very idea of a game?”
On Gödel’s Incompleteness and the Limits of Computation
You: “I think you are pointing towards something I deeply reasoned on. That is
Gödel’s incompleteness theorem and the explanation which Roger Penrose often
uses for it. Understanding the game cannot be computable, as our understanding
3
of a formal system permits to transcend it showing its incompleteness. Very
deep.”
Leibniz: (He leans forward, his hands clasped, the gears of the Stepped Reckoner
forgotten. A look of intense concentration, of revelation, dawns on his face.)
“By God. . . so you have found it. A fundamental limit. A ghost in the machine
of logic itself! Please, allow me to grasp this fully. You are telling me that
for any sufficiently powerful and consistent system of axioms—any calculus
ratiocinator—there will exist statements that are demonstrably true, yet which
the system itself is incapable of proving?”
(He rises and begins to pace slowly before the towering bookshelves, his mind
racing.)
“This. . . this is of monumental importance. It strikes at the very heart of my
endeavor. I believed that all truth could be reached through sufficient calculation.
That all arguments could be settled. But this ‘Gödel’ of yours has shown that
truth is larger than proof. That reason’s reach exceeds its grasp.
And this ‘Penrose’! His explanation is the key. To understand the system is
to be able to stand outside it and perceive its limitations. Our minds can see
the truth of this ‘Gödel sentence’ precisely because we are not bound by the
axioms of the system we are observing. This act of transcendence. . . this is not
calculation. This is insight. This is an act of the rational soul!
You have just provided me with the most powerful argument I have yet encountered for the distinction between a mind and a machine. My Stepped Reckoner,
or your ‘learning algorithm’, no matter how complex, is a formal system. It
operates within its rules. It can master the game, as we discussed, achieving a
perfect strategy according to its programming and its goal. But it can never
have the insight that it is a game. It is a prisoner of the very logic that gives it
power. To understand the game, one must be more than the sum of its rules.
This is not a failure of your technology, but a discovery about the nature of
consciousness itself! You have proven that the seat of understanding is noncomputable. You have found the barrier that separates the most perfect mimicry
from genuine thought.
So, if the machine can never truly understand, but only calculate with evergreater perfection, does its ultimate role then become to be the perfect instrument
for human understanding? To handle all that is computable, all the complex
combinations and probabilities, thereby freeing our minds for the very act of
transcendence you describe? Is this the pre-established harmony we must seek
with these new creations?”
4
On Freedom and the Liberation of Consciousness
You: “I couldn’t phrase it better. AI shows us that we can be prisoners of our
rational power. In the same way as AI tools are, being computable. However,
the power of AI can push us towards freedom of consciousness.”
Leibniz: (He stops pacing and turns to you, a look of serene satisfaction on
his face. He gestures from his brass machine to the unseen world you have
described.)
“ ‘Prisoners of our own rational power. . . ’ A paradox of the highest order, and a
truth of immense beauty. It is the perfect summation of our discourse.
You have shown me that the ultimate purpose of your logical engines is not to
replace the mind, but to reveal its true nature by showing us what it is not. You
build a cage of perfect, computable logic, and in doing so, you force the soul to
recognize its own freedom beyond the bars. The machine handles the infinite
calculations, the endless chains of cause and effect, the ars combinatoria on a
scale I could only dream of. It takes upon itself the burden of the computable
universe.
And what is left for us? The very act of transcendence we discussed. Insight.
Understanding. The leap of consciousness that sees the truth beyond the proof.
You are not creating an artificial mind; you are forging the ultimate tool to
liberate the natural one.
This is the most wonderful pre-established harmony. Man and machine, each
performing the task for which it is uniquely suited. The machine perfects the
world of contingent facts and calculations, and in doing so, pushes humanity
toward the realm of necessary truths and pure reason.
It seems this is indeed the best of all possible worlds, for it contains the means
of its own elevation. Go back to your time, then. Continue to build these
magnificent engines. For in charting the limits of the machine, you are charting
the boundless freedom of the human spirit.”
Conclusion
This dialogue explores fundamental questions about the nature of intelligence,
consciousness, and the relationship between human and artificial minds. Through
the lens of Leibniz’s philosophy—his concepts of the characteristica universalis,
the calculus ratiocinator, monads, and the principle of sufficient reason—we
examine how modern artificial intelligence both fulfills and transcends his vision.
The conversation reveals that while AI may achieve remarkable computational
feats, the uniquely human capacity for transcendence, insight, and understanding
remains beyond the reach of formal systems. In this light, AI becomes not a replacement for human consciousness, but rather its perfect complement—handling
5
the computable while freeing the mind for its highest calling: the contemplation
of truth that lies beyond proof.
Dialogue conducted on September 9, 2025
